name: Hash Maps and Sets
author: Recurse
subject: swe
description: Hashing for interviews: counting, complement lookup, sets for membership, grouping keys, and when sorting is the better trade.

lesson.intro: Hash maps are the most useful data structure in coding interviews: they turn "search for it" into "look it up". This pack shows how they work inside, then drills the four patterns behind most hash map problems: counting, complement lookup, membership with sets, and grouping by a canonical key.
objectives: Explain how hashing, buckets, collisions and resizing give average O(1) operations, and when that degrades to O(n)
Apply the counting, complement lookup, set membership and grouping patterns to new problems
Choose safe keys in Python and JavaScript, avoiding unhashable and identity-compared keys
Decide when sorting is a better trade-off than a hash map

sections.title: How a hash map gets O(1) lookups
sections.body:
Imagine checking whether a new username is taken among 10 million existing ones. Scanning a list means up to 10 million comparisons. A hash map answers in about the same time whether it holds ten names or ten million.

A **hash function** turns a key into an integer, its **hash**. The map takes that number modulo the number of **buckets** to pick a slot, so a lookup goes straight to one bucket instead of scanning everything. The same key always produces the same hash, which is how you find it again later.

Different keys sometimes land in the same bucket. That is a **collision**, and every hash table has a plan for it. **Chaining** keeps a small list in each bucket. **Open addressing**, which Python's dict uses, probes other slots until it finds a free one. Either way, a lookup only examines the few keys that share a bucket.

To keep those groups small, the table tracks its **load factor**: entries divided by buckets. When it passes a threshold (commonly somewhere around 0.66 to 0.75), the table allocates more buckets and reinserts every key, because each key's bucket depends on the bucket count. That resize is O(n), but it happens rarely enough that inserts stay O(1) on average, the same amortized argument as appending to a dynamic array.

What you get in each language:

- Python `dict` maps keys to values and `set` stores keys only. Keys must be hashable: numbers, strings, and tuples of hashable items. Lists, dicts and sets are not.
- JavaScript `Map` and `Set` accept any value as a key and remember insertion order. Plain objects (`{}`) also work as maps, but their keys are always converted to strings, so `obj[1]` and `obj["1"]` are the same entry.
- In a JavaScript `Map`, objects and arrays are compared by identity, not contents. `map.get([1, 2])` with a fresh array never finds an entry stored under a different `[1, 2]` array.

The toy class below is a working chained hash map in about 30 lines. Read `put`, `get` and `_resize`: that is the whole idea.
sections.pitfall: Mutable keys. Python refuses lists (`TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`), and JavaScript happily accepts arrays as Map keys but matches them by identity, so lookups with an equal-looking array silently miss. Use a tuple in Python and a string such as `key.join(",")` in JavaScript.

activity.title: Watch keys land in buckets
activity.prompt: Insert a few short words and note which bucket each one lands in. Keep going until two keys collide and the load factor passes 0.75, then resize and notice that keys move to different buckets because the bucket count changed.

check.question: Why does a hash map lookup usually take O(1) time even with a million keys?
choices: It keeps the keys sorted and uses binary search
The hash picks one bucket directly, and each bucket holds only a few keys on average
It caches the results of recent lookups
check.explanation: Hashing jumps straight to one bucket, and resizing keeps the load factor low so buckets stay small. Collisions do happen, which is why buckets can hold more than one key; binary search would be O(log n), not O(1).

sections.title: Counting with frequency maps
sections.body:
"Is `listen` an anagram of `silent`?" "Which word appears most often in this log?" "Does every character appear an even number of times?" All three are counting problems, and a map from item to count solves each of them in one pass.

The move is the same in every language: read the current count (default 0), add one, store it back.

- Python: `counts[x] = counts.get(x, 0) + 1`, or `collections.Counter(items)`, which runs the whole loop for you. `defaultdict(int)` is another option: missing keys start at 0.
- JavaScript: `counts.set(x, (counts.get(x) ?? 0) + 1)` with a `Map`.

Trace counting the letters of `"banana"`: b becomes 1, a becomes 1, n becomes 1, a becomes 2, n becomes 2, a becomes 3. The final map is `{b: 1, a: 3, n: 2}`, built in O(n) time.

**Valid anagram** follows directly: two strings are anagrams exactly when their letter counts match. Count up for the first string and down for the second; if a count would go below zero, the second string has a letter the first ran out of. A length check up front rejects many inputs instantly. The alternative is to sort both strings and compare, `sorted(s) == sorted(t)`, which is O(n log n) and very short to write. In an interview, mention both and say why counting is faster.

How much space does counting take? O(k), where k is the number of distinct keys. For lowercase English letters k is at most 26, so many interviewers accept O(1) space. For arbitrary Unicode text or integers, the map can grow with the input, so say O(n).
sections.pitfall: Reading `counts[x]` for a key that was never stored raises `KeyError` in Python (unless you use `get`, `Counter` or `defaultdict`), and returns `undefined` from a JavaScript Map, which turns `+ 1` into `NaN`.

check.question: What is the time complexity of deciding whether two strings of length n are anagrams by counting letters with a map?
check.explanation: Each string is scanned once and every map operation is O(1) on average, so the total is O(n). Sorting both strings and comparing is the O(n log n) alternative.

sections.title: Complement lookup: have I already seen what I need?
sections.body:
Two sum is the most famous interview question for a reason. Given `nums` and a `target`, find two positions whose values add up to the target. The brute force checks every pair: O(n^2).

Flip the question around. Standing at `nums[i]`, you do not need to search for a partner, because you know exactly which value would work: `target - nums[i]`, its **complement**. The only question is whether you have already seen it, and a map from value to index answers that in O(1).

Trace with `nums = [3, 8, 4, 5]` and `target = 9`:

- i = 0, value 3: need 6, not seen. Store 3 at index 0.
- i = 1, value 8: need 1, not seen. Store 8 at index 1.
- i = 2, value 4: need 5, not seen. Store 4 at index 2.
- i = 3, value 5: need 4, seen at index 2. Return [2, 3].

One pass, O(n) time, O(n) space. Notice the order inside the loop: check first, then store. If you store first, a target of 6 with a 3 in the array pairs the 3 with itself.

This move generalizes to any problem shaped like "find an earlier thing that combines with the current thing". The most important variation uses prefix sums. To count subarrays that sum to k, keep a running prefix sum and a map from each prefix sum to how many times it has appeared. A subarray ending at the current position sums to k exactly when some earlier prefix equals `prefix - k`. Starting the map as `{0: 1}` counts subarrays that begin at index 0. Unlike the sliding window technique, this works with negative numbers.
sections.code:
def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}                        # value -> index
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        need = target - x
        if need in seen:             # check before storing
            return [seen[need], i]
        seen[x] = i
    return []

def count_subarrays_with_sum(nums, k):
    counts = {0: 1}                  # prefix sum -> times seen
    prefix = 0
    total = 0
    for x in nums:
        prefix += x
        total += counts.get(prefix - k, 0)
        counts[prefix] = counts.get(prefix, 0) + 1
    return total

print(two_sum([3, 8, 4, 5], 9))                      # [2, 3]
print(count_subarrays_with_sum([1, 2, 1, 2, 1], 3))  # 4
sections.pitfall: Storing before checking. With `seen[x] = i` above the lookup, `two_sum([3, 4], 6)` finds 3's complement (another 3) in the map immediately and returns [0, 0], using one element twice.

activity.title: Trace prefix sums with a map
activity.prompt: Run it and match each printed line to a subarray that sums to 3. Then switch to the negative-number case in the task and predict the count before you run it.

props.code:
def count_subarrays_with_sum(nums, k):
    counts = {0: 1}
    prefix = 0
    total = 0
    for x in nums:
        prefix += x
        found = counts.get(prefix - k, 0)
        total += found
        counts[prefix] = counts.get(prefix, 0) + 1
        print(f"x={x}, prefix={prefix}, look for {prefix - k}: found {found}")
    return total

print(count_subarrays_with_sum([1, 2, 1, 2, 1], 3))
props.task: Change the last line to call count_subarrays_with_sum([1, -1, 1, -1], 0). Predict the final count first.
props.expectOutput:
x=1, prefix=1, look for 1: found 0
x=-1, prefix=0, look for 0: found 1
x=1, prefix=1, look for 1: found 1
x=-1, prefix=0, look for 0: found 2
4

check.question: One-pass two sum runs on nums = [2, 11, 7, 15] with target 9. What does the map hold at the moment the answer is found?
check.explanation: 2 and 11 are stored at indexes 0 and 1. At index 2 the value is 7, its complement 2 is already in the map, so the function returns [0, 2] before 7 is ever stored.

sections.title: Sets for membership, and the start-of-run trick
sections.body:
Sometimes you do not need a value attached to a key, only the answer to "is it there?". That is a **set**: a hash map with keys and no values. Membership tests, inserts and deletes are O(1) on average, compared with O(n) for `x in some_list`.

**Contains duplicate** is the simplest example. Walk the array, and before adding each item to a set, check whether it is already there. You can stop at the first repeat. The one-liner `len(set(nums)) != len(nums)` is also O(n), but it always processes the whole array.

A more interesting example is **longest consecutive sequence**. In `[100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2]` the longest run of consecutive integers is 1, 2, 3, 4, so the answer is 4. Sorting first solves it in O(n log n). With a set you can reach O(n) using one idea: **only start counting at the beginning of a run**. A number x starts a run exactly when x - 1 is not in the set.

Trace it with the set {100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2}:

- 100: 99 is missing, so 100 starts a run. 101 is missing too. Length 1.
- 4: 3 is present, so 4 is not a start. Skip it.
- 200: 199 is missing, so it starts a run of length 1.
- 1: 0 is missing, so it starts a run. Walk to 2, 3, 4 (all present); 5 is missing. Length 4.
- 3 and 2: their predecessors are present. Skip.

Why is this O(n) with a while loop inside a for loop? Each number is walked over at most once, from the start of its own run, so the inner steps add up to at most n across the whole outer loop. Amortized arguments like this come up often: count the total work across the loop, not the worst single iteration times n.

Loop over the set rather than the original array, so duplicates in the input do not repeat a walk.
sections.pitfall: Without the start-of-run check, every number walks its whole run, and an input such as 1 to n becomes O(n^2). The check is what makes the solution linear.

activity.title: Longest consecutive sequence
activity.prompt: Use the start-of-run test from the trace: only walk upward from x when x - 1 is missing. Test an empty array and an input with duplicates before you submit.

check.question: In the set-based longest consecutive sequence solution, when does the code walk upward from a number x?
choices: For every number in the array
Only when x + 1 is in the set
Only when x - 1 is not in the set
Only for the smallest number in the array
check.explanation: x starts a run exactly when its predecessor is missing. Walking from every number is correct but quadratic in the worst case, and the smallest number only starts one of possibly many runs.

sections.title: Grouping by a canonical key
sections.body:
Given `["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"]`, group the anagrams together: `[["eat", "tea", "ate"], ["tan", "nat"], ["bat"]]`. Comparing every pair of words takes O(n^2) comparisons. Instead, give every word a **canonical key**: a value that is identical for all words that belong together and different otherwise. A map from key to list of words then does the grouping in one pass.

Two good keys for anagrams:

- **Sorted letters**: `"".join(sorted(word))`, so "eat", "tea" and "ate" all become "aet". This costs O(k log k) per word of length k.
- **Letter-count signature**: a tuple of 26 counts. This costs O(k) per word, a bit faster for long words, at the price of more code.

Trace with sorted keys: eat goes to aet, tea to aet, tan to ant, ate to aet, nat to ant, bat to abt. The map ends as aet: [eat, tea, ate], ant: [tan, nat], abt: [bat], and the answer is its values. Total cost: O(n k log k) for n words.

The same idea solves many problems: group words by length, group log lines by user ID, find duplicate files by hashing their contents, group dates by (year, month). Whenever a problem says "group", ask what key would make items in the same group identical.

Language details matter here. In Python the key must be hashable, so use a string or a tuple, never a list. In JavaScript use a string key (the sorted letters joined, or the counts joined with `#`), because a Map compares array keys by identity and every word would end up in its own group.
sections.pitfall: Using a list as the key: `groups[sorted(w)]` raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`. Join the sorted letters into a string or wrap them in `tuple()`.

check.question: Which key correctly groups anagrams in a Python dict?
check.explanation: The joined sorted letters are a hashable string that is equal exactly for anagrams. sorted(word) is a list and cannot be a key. frozenset is hashable but forgets repeated letters, so "aab" and "abb" would collide. Length groups unrelated words.

sections.title: Average versus worst case, and when sorting wins
sections.body:
"O(1)" for hash maps is an average-case promise. It assumes the hash function spreads keys evenly across buckets. If many keys collide, a bucket's chain or probe sequence grows, and in the worst case, with every key in one bucket, each lookup is O(n) and building the map is O(n^2).

This is not only theoretical. Attackers have slowed web servers to a crawl by sending thousands of request parameters crafted to collide, an attack called **hash flooding**. That is why Python randomizes string hashes per process (`hash("abc")` changes between runs) and why modern languages use hash functions designed to resist it. For interviews: quote O(1) average for map operations, and mention the O(n) worst case if asked or if inputs could be adversarial.

Hash maps also have costs that Big-O hides. They use noticeably more memory than a plain array, and they do not keep keys sorted. Python dicts and JavaScript Maps preserve insertion order, which is not the same thing.

So keep **sorting** in mind as the alternative:

- Sorting costs O(n log n) time but can use little extra space, and it puts equal items next to each other, so duplicates and groups can be found by scanning neighbors.
- If you need sorted output anyway, or you plan to use two pointers afterward (as in 3sum), sort.
- If memory is tight or the input is already sorted, sorting-based approaches win.

**Top k frequent elements** shows the trade-off nicely. Count with a map in O(n), then pick the k most frequent values:

- Sort the distinct values by count: O(u log u), where u is the number of distinct values. Simple and usually fine.
- Keep a heap of size k: O(u log k), better when k is much smaller than u. `Counter.most_common(k)` does this for you.
- **Bucket by frequency**: a list where index f holds the values that appear exactly f times. No value can appear more than n times, so n + 1 buckets suffice, and walking them from high to low is O(n) in total.
sections.code:
from collections import Counter
import heapq

def top_k_sorted(nums, k):
    counts = Counter(nums)                                   # O(n)
    by_count = sorted(counts, key=counts.get, reverse=True)  # O(u log u)
    return by_count[:k]

def top_k_heap(nums, k):
    counts = Counter(nums)
    return heapq.nlargest(k, counts, key=counts.get)         # O(u log k)

nums = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3]
print(top_k_sorted(nums, 2))   # [1, 2]
print(top_k_heap(nums, 2))     # [1, 2]
# u = number of distinct values, at most n
sections.pitfall: Calling a hash map solution O(1) space. A map that may hold every input item is O(n) space; only a small fixed key set, such as 26 letters, makes it O(1).

check.question: When is sorting a better choice than a hash map for detecting duplicates?
choices: When the input is huge and must be processed in O(n) time
When you need each check to take O(1) time
When extra memory is very limited and O(n log n) time is acceptable
check.explanation: An in-place sort needs little extra memory and brings duplicates next to each other, at the cost of O(n log n) time. If you need O(n) time, the hash set is the right tool, and strings work fine as hash keys.

sections.title: Practice: spotting hash map problems
sections.body:
Hash map problems announce themselves once you know the signals:

- "Have I seen this before?" (duplicates, first repeated item, visited states): a set.
- "How many times?" (frequency, majority, anagrams, most common): a counting map.
- "Find an earlier item that combines with this one" (two sum, subarray sum equals k): complement lookup, often with prefix sums.
- "Group these by something" (anagrams, same category): a map from canonical key to list.
- "Do it in O(n)" when the obvious solution sorts or uses nested loops: a hash map is the usual way to trade memory for time.

And the classic mistakes interviewers watch for:

- Storing before checking in complement problems, so an element pairs with itself.
- Mutable or identity-compared keys: lists in Python, arrays or objects in a JavaScript Map.
- Forgetting the default for missing keys (`KeyError`, or `undefined + 1` becoming `NaN`).
- Claiming O(1) space for a map that grows with the input.
- Adding or removing keys while iterating over a dict, which raises `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` in Python.

When you explain a hash map solution, say what the keys are, what the values are, and what question the map answers in O(1). "A map from value to index, so I can ask whether the complement has appeared" is exactly the kind of sentence interviewers want to hear.

The code below shows the three core patterns in JavaScript, so you can use whichever language your interview allows.

activity.title: Top k frequent elements
activity.prompt: Count with a map first. Then try the bucket idea: a list where index f holds the values that appear f times, walked from the highest frequency down until you have k values.

check.question: A problem asks for the first character in a string that never repeats. Which approach is O(n) and correct?
choices: Count characters in one pass, then scan the string again and return the first with count 1
For each character, count its occurrences with s.count(ch)
Sort the string and look for characters that differ from both neighbors
Add characters to a set and return the first one that was not already in it
check.explanation: Two linear passes: build the counts, then find the first position whose count is 1. s.count inside a loop is O(n^2), sorting loses the original order, and the set version returns the first character immediately, before you know whether it repeats later.

keyTerms.definition: A function that turns a key into an integer; equal keys must always produce the same hash.
A slot in a hash table's internal array, chosen by hash modulo the number of buckets.
Two different keys mapping to the same bucket, handled by chaining or open addressing.
Entries divided by buckets; when it passes a threshold the table resizes and reinserts every key.
A hash-based collection of unique keys with no values, used for O(1) average membership tests.
A map from each item to how many times it appears, built in one pass.
The value that would complete the current item, such as target - x in two sum.
A key that is equal for exactly the items that belong in the same group, such as sorted letters for anagrams.
An attack that sends many colliding keys to push hash table operations toward their O(n) worst case.

summary: A hash map turns a key into a bucket index, so lookups, inserts and deletes are O(1) on average and O(n) in the worst case.
Counting maps answer "how many" and sets answer "have I seen it"; both work in one pass.
Complement lookup turns "search for a partner" into "have I already seen target - x", making pair problems O(n).
Grouping needs a canonical key, such as sorted letters, that is equal exactly for items in the same group.
Keys must be immutable in Python; in JavaScript use string keys in a Map instead of arrays.
Sorting is the O(n log n) alternative when memory is tight, order matters, or two pointers come next.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend how a hash map can find one name among ten million almost instantly, what happens when two names land in the same bucket, and why two sum gets faster when you remember the numbers you have already seen.

questions.question: What is the average time complexity of looking up a key in a Python dict or a JavaScript Map with n entries?
questions.explanation: The hash points straight at one bucket, and resizing keeps buckets small, so lookups are O(1) on average. O(log n) is what a balanced search tree or binary search gives.

questions.question: A hash table has 8 buckets and holds 6 entries. What is its load factor? Answer as a decimal.
questions.explanation: Load factor = entries / buckets = 6 / 8 = 0.75. Many tables resize around this point to keep collisions rare.

questions.question: What does a hash table do when its load factor passes the resize threshold?
choices: It sorts the keys so it can use binary search
It allocates more buckets and reinserts every key into its new bucket
It deletes the oldest keys to make room
questions.explanation: A bucket index is hash modulo the bucket count, so after growing the array every key must be placed again. The resize is O(n), but it is rare, so inserts remain O(1) amortized.

questions.question: What does this JavaScript log?
questions.explanation: Map compares object and array keys by identity. The array passed to get is a new array, not the one used in set, so there is no match and get returns undefined. Use a string key such as "1,2" instead.

questions.question: What does this JavaScript log?
questions.code:
const obj = {}
obj[1] = "number"
obj["1"] = "string"
console.log(Object.keys(obj).length, obj[1])
questions.explanation: Plain object keys are converted to strings, so 1 and "1" are the same key and the second assignment overwrites the first. A Map would keep 1 and "1" as separate keys.

questions.question: This code raises an error on the last line. What is the problem?
choices: Lists are unhashable; use a tuple such as (3, 4) as the key
The dict must be created with dict() instead of {}
Dict keys must be strings, so the key needs str()
questions.explanation: Python raises TypeError: unhashable type: 'list', because a list could change after insertion and its hash would no longer match its bucket. Tuples are immutable and hashable. Keys do not have to be strings; ints and tuples are common keys.

questions.question: Fill the blank so the function counts how many times each character appears.
questions.explanation: get(ch, 0) returns 0 for a character seen for the first time, so adding 1 works every time. counts[ch] raises KeyError on a new key, get(ch) returns None and None + 1 raises TypeError, and get(ch, 1) never increments.

questions.question: You count the letters of "mississippi" in a dict. How many keys does the dict have at the end?
questions.explanation: The distinct letters are m, i, s and p. Counts: m 1, i 4, s 4, p 2. The number of keys is the number of distinct items, which is what the map's space depends on.

questions.question: What does this JavaScript log?
questions.explanation: The first get("a") returns undefined, and undefined + 1 is NaN. NaN + 1 is still NaN. Write (counts.get(w) ?? 0) + 1 to default missing keys to 0.

questions.question: Which approaches correctly decide whether two lowercase strings s and t are anagrams? Select all that apply.
choices: Equal lengths and equal sums of the letter codes
Count up for s, count down for t, and check that every count ends at 0
questions.explanation: Sorting and counting both compare the full multiset of letters. Sets ignore how often a letter appears ("aab" and "abb" have the same set). Code sums collide easily: "ad" and "bc" both sum to 197.

questions.question: When can a letter-counting map fairly be called O(1) space, and when is it O(n)?
questions.answer: It is O(1) when the possible keys form a small fixed set, such as the 26 lowercase letters. When keys can be arbitrary values, such as any integer or any Unicode character, the map can grow with the input, so it is O(n).
questions.explanation: Space depends on the number of distinct keys, not on n directly. Say which case you are in when you state complexity.

questions.question: One-pass two sum (check the complement, then store the value) runs on nums = [4, 1, 6, 3] with target 7. What does it return?
questions.explanation: 4 is stored, then 1 is stored. At index 2 the value 6 needs 1, which is in the map at index 1, so it returns [1, 2]. 4 + 3 also makes 7, but the scan reaches 6 first and returns the first pair it completes.

questions.question: two_sum([3, 4, 2], 6) should return [1, 2] but returns [0, 0]. What is the bug?
choices: The loop should run in reverse so partners appear later
target - x should be x - target
It stores x before checking, so 3 finds itself as its own complement
enumerate starts counting at 1, so the indexes are off
questions.explanation: At index 0, 3 is stored first; then 6 - 3 = 3 is in the map, pointing at index 0. Checking the complement before storing the current value makes sure an element can only pair with an earlier one.

questions.question: Fill the blank so the function counts subarrays whose sum is exactly k.
questions.explanation: A subarray from just after an earlier prefix p up to here sums to prefix - p. That equals k exactly when p = prefix - k, so you count how many earlier prefixes had that value. k - prefix has the sign flipped.

questions.question: What does count_subarrays_with_sum([1, 1, 1], 2) return?
questions.explanation: The subarrays [1, 1] at indexes 0 to 1 and [1, 1] at indexes 1 to 2 both sum to 2. In the trace, prefixes are 1, 2, 3; prefix 2 finds the starting 0 and prefix 3 finds the earlier 1.

questions.question: Why does count_subarrays_with_sum start its map as {0: 1} instead of an empty map?
choices: So subarrays that start at index 0 are counted: they need an earlier prefix sum of 0
To avoid a KeyError on the first lookup
Because an empty subarray always sums to k
So that negative numbers are handled correctly
questions.explanation: A subarray covering nums[0..i] sums to prefix itself, which equals k only if the "earlier prefix" is 0, the empty prefix before index 0. The lookup uses get with a default, so there is no KeyError risk either way.

questions.question: Put the steps inside the loop of one-pass two sum in order.
items: Look up need in the map
If it is there, return its stored index and i
Otherwise store nums[i] with index i
questions.explanation: Checking before storing guarantees the partner comes from an earlier index, so no element pairs with itself.

questions.question: You will test whether values are present 10,000 times against a collection of 100,000 items. Which collection makes each test O(1) on average?
choices: A sorted list searched with in
questions.explanation: A set hashes the value and checks one bucket. The in operator on a list or tuple scans every item, and it does not use binary search even when the list is sorted.

questions.question: What is the length of the longest consecutive sequence in [9, 1, 4, 7, 3, -1, 0, 5, 8, -1, 6]?
questions.explanation: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 are all present, which is 7 numbers. The other run, -1, 0, 1, stops because 2 is missing. The duplicate -1 does not matter.

questions.question: The longest consecutive sequence solution has a while loop inside a for loop. Why is it still O(n)?
choices: The while loop runs at most 26 times
The inner loop only runs for the smallest number
Each number is walked over at most once, from the start of its own run, so inner steps total at most n
questions.explanation: The start-of-run check means a run is walked exactly once, from its first number. Summed over all runs, the inner loop takes at most n steps, so the whole thing is O(n). Several numbers can start runs, not only the smallest.

questions.question: Fill the blank so this runs in O(n).
questions.explanation: Only numbers whose predecessor is missing start a run, so each run is walked once. x - 1 in present would walk from the middle of runs and miss their starts; x not in present is never true.

questions.question: How does `len(set(nums)) != len(nums)` compare with a loop that returns True at the first repeated value?
choices: Both are O(n), but the loop can stop early when a duplicate appears near the start
The loop version is O(n log n)
Only the set version works with negative numbers
questions.explanation: Both do O(n) average work with hashing. The one-liner always builds the full set, while the loop returns as soon as it sees a repeat, which can be much faster on inputs with an early duplicate.

questions.question: With key = "".join(sorted(word)), which pair of words lands in the same group?
questions.explanation: listen and silent both sort to "eilnst". The other pairs differ in at least one character or count, so their sorted keys differ.

questions.question: groupAnagrams(["eat", "tea"]) returns [["eat"], ["tea"]] instead of one group. What is wrong?
choices: sort() puts the letters in descending order
The key is an array, and Map compares arrays by identity; join the letters into a string
[...w] splits the string into words, not letters
groups.get(key) returns a copy, so the push is lost
questions.explanation: Each iteration creates a new array, so has(key) is always false and every word gets its own group. [...w].sort().join("") gives the string "aet" for both words, and strings compare by value.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of grouping n words, each up to k letters long, using sorted letters as the key?
questions.explanation: Each word is sorted in O(k log k) and the map insert is O(k) to hash a k-letter key, so n words cost O(n k log k). A 26-count signature key brings it down to O(n k).

questions.question: Match each grouping problem with a good canonical key.

pairs.right: A hash of the file's bytes

pairs.left: Group points on the same horizontal line

questions.explanation: A canonical key is equal exactly for items that belong together. Month alone would merge January 2024 with January 2025, which is why the tuple includes the year.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time for a single lookup in a hash map holding n keys?
questions.explanation: If every key collides into one bucket, a lookup has to examine all n of them. Good hash functions and resizing make this extremely unlikely in practice, which is why the average is O(1).

questions.question: Which are good reasons to sort instead of using a hash map? Select all that apply.
choices: You need the output in sorted order anyway
Memory is tight and O(n log n) time is acceptable
You plan to use two pointers on the result
You need O(1) average lookups by key
questions.explanation: Sorting gives order, low extra memory and the setup for two pointers, and it is free when the input is already sorted. O(1) average lookups by key are the hash map's strength, not sorting's.

questions.question: In the bucket approach to top k frequent elements over n numbers, why are n + 1 buckets (indexes 0 to n) enough?
choices: No value can appear more than n times, so every frequency fits
There are at most n distinct values
k is never larger than n
Each bucket holds exactly one value
questions.explanation: Bucket index = frequency, and frequencies range from 1 to n. It is true that there are at most n distinct values, but that bounds what goes in the buckets, not how many buckets you need. Several values can share a bucket.

questions.question: Why can hash("abc") give a different number each time you start Python?
questions.answer: Python randomizes string hashing with a per-process seed, so attackers cannot precompute many keys that collide (hash flooding) and push dict operations toward their O(n) worst case.
questions.explanation: The hash only needs to be consistent within one run. Randomizing it between runs protects servers that put untrusted input, such as request parameters, into dicts.

questions.question: Given a list of words, return True if any two of them are anagrams of each other. Which approach is efficient and correct?
choices: Sort the list alphabetically and compare neighbors
Compare every pair of words with sorted()
Count all the letters across all words together
Build each word's sorted-letter key and report a repeat in a set
questions.explanation: Two words are anagrams exactly when their canonical keys match, so a set of keys finds a repeat in one pass: O(n k log k). Alphabetical order does not put anagrams next to each other, and comparing all pairs is O(n^2) comparisons.

questions.question: Match each question you ask inside a loop with the structure that answers it in O(1).

pairs.left: Have I seen this value before?
How many times has each value occurred?
Is target - x already stored, and where?
pairs.right: A map from value to index
A map from canonical key to list

questions.explanation: Naming the question the map answers is the fastest way to pick the structure, and it is the sentence interviewers want to hear when you explain your plan.

questions.question: This code raises RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration. What is the fix?
choices: Iterate over a snapshot such as list(counts), or build a new dict with a comprehension
Replace del counts[key] with counts[key] = None
Dicts cannot hold zero values, so start the counts at 1
questions.explanation: Deleting a key changes the dict while the loop is walking it, which Python forbids. Looping over list(counts) iterates a copy of the keys, and {k: v for k, v in counts.items() if v} builds the filtered dict in one go. Setting None hides the problem rather than removing keys.
